questions.question: What is SLF4J and why is it used instead of logging directly with a framework?
questions.title: What Is SLF4J in Java Logging
questions.direct_answer: **SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java)** is an **abstraction/facade**, not a logging implementation. Your code calls the SLF4J API (`Logger`, `log.info`), and at runtime a real backend like **Logback** or **Log4j2** does the actual logging. The benefit: you can **swap the implementation without changing code**, and libraries that all use SLF4J unify under one configuration.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **SLF4J = facade/abstraction**, not an implementation.
- Code uses `org.slf4j.Logger`; **Logback/Log4j2** does the real work at runtime.
- **Swap implementations with no code change** (change the dependency).
- **Logback** is SLF4J's native backend and the **Spring Boot default**.
- A shared API means **all libraries unify under one configuration**.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: SLF4J stands for Simple Logging Facade for Java, and the key word is facade — it's an abstraction layer, not a logging implementation itself. Your code calls the SLF4J API, things like LoggerFactory.getLogger and log.info, but SLF4J doesn't actually write the logs. At runtime, a real logging library is plugged in behind it — usually Logback, sometimes Log4j2, or java.util.logging — and that's what does the actual work of formatting and writing the output. It's the facade design pattern applied to logging. The reason you'd use it instead of logging directly with a framework is decoupling. Because your code and all the libraries you depend on are written against the single SLF4J API, you can swap the underlying implementation without changing a line of your code — you just change which library is on the classpath. So if you start with Logback and later decide you want Log4j2 for its async performance, your application code stays exactly the same. The other big win is unification: every well-behaved library logs through SLF4J too, so all of those logs flow through your one logging configuration instead of each library doing its own thing. In practice, in a Spring Boot app, SLF4J is the API you code against and Logback is the implementation that comes by default, so you get the facade and a solid backend out of the box. One thing to be careful about is not importing the implementation classes directly — you only import from org.slf4j in your code, otherwise you've broken the decoupling that's the whole point.

sections.title: The logging API and provider are separate layers
sections.content:
Application code depends on the **SLF4J API**, which defines `Logger` and methods such as `info`, `warn`, and `error`. A provider on the runtime classpath—commonly Logback or Log4j 2—implements those calls, formats the event, applies level rules, and writes to the configured destinations.

For example, `log.info("Created order {}", orderId)` stays unchanged if a project replaces one provider with another. The same facade also lets libraries send events through the application’s chosen logging setup. SLF4J does not write files by itself. A project should normally have one compatible provider; missing or competing providers lead to warnings or unexpected behavior. Parameter placeholders also avoid building messages when their level is disabled.

sections.title: How SLF4J Sits in the Stack
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB Code[Your code + libraries
log.info via SLF4J API] --> SLF4J[SLF4J facade] SLF4J --> Bind{Binding at runtime} Bind --> LB[Logback
Spring Boot default] Bind --> L4J[Log4j2] Bind --> JUL[java.util.logging] ```

sections.title: Code Depends Only on the SLF4J API
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking SLF4J logs**: it doesn't; it delegates to a bound implementation like Logback.
- **Importing the implementation**: importing `ch.qos.logback...` in app code defeats the decoupling — only import `org.slf4j`.
- **Multiple bindings**: putting two implementations on the classpath triggers the classic SLF4J multiple-bindings warning.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: SLF4J keeps application and library code independent of one logging provider. The runtime still needs one compatible provider, and provider-specific appenders and configuration remain tied to that choice. Check the dependency graph when switching so old bridges or a second provider do not remain.

questions.question: How do you create and use a Logger in Java with SLF4J?
questions.title: Creating and Using a Logger with SLF4J
questions.direct_answer: Create a logger with `LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class)` and call parameterized methods such as `log.info("Created order {}", orderId)`. A `private static final` field is the common one-logger-per-class convention, not a correctness requirement. Passing the declaring class gives the logger a stable class/package name for configuration.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class)` creates a class-named logger
- `private static final` is the common shared-field convention, not a correctness requirement
- The class/package name supports targeted level configuration
- `{}` placeholders separate the template from its argument values
- Pass a `Throwable` when this event should preserve its stack trace

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I obtain an SLF4J logger with `LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class)`. I commonly store it in a `private static final` field so instances share the reference and it is not reassigned, although an instance field is also valid. Passing the declaring class gives a stable name that follows the package hierarchy. I write parameterized events such as `log.info("Created order {}", orderId)`, which lets the provider skip formatting when the event is disabled. For an unexpected failure, I pass the exception object at the layer responsible for recording it: `log.error("Order {} failed", orderId, ex)`.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
SLF4J loggers are obtained from `LoggerFactory`. Passing `OrderService.class` names the logger after that class, so package or class-level configuration can select it.

A common declaration is `private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);`. `static final` avoids storing an identical logger reference in every instance and prevents reassignment, but SLF4J also supports instance logger fields. The important part is a stable, accurate logger name.

Use parameterized calls such as `log.info("Created order {}", orderId)` instead of concatenating values. Pass an exception object when its stack trace belongs on the event: `log.error("Order {} failed", orderId, ex)`.

sections.title: Why Each Keyword
sections.content:
blue|static|~One per class|shared by all instances|not created per object|cheap
emerald|final|~Never reassigned|safe constant|immutable reference|convention
amber|MyClass.class|~Package-named logger|enables per-package config|matches hierarchy|no typos
rose|{} placeholders|~Performance|no string build when off|cleaner code|null-safe

sections.title: Declaring and Using a Logger
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Non-static logger**: `private final Logger log = ...` per instance creates needless objects; use `static`.
- **Hardcoded name**: `getLogger("PaymentService")` as a string breaks on rename and loses package config; use `PaymentService.class`.
- **Concatenation**: `log.debug("x=" + obj)` builds the string even when DEBUG is off; use `log.debug("x={}", obj)`.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A class-based logger name works naturally with package configuration. A deliberate business-category logger can be useful in rare cases, but it separates the event from the source class. Static versus instance storage has little bearing on correctness; follow the project's convention and keep the name accurate.

questions.question: How do you configure logging in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Logging Configuration in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: When a Spring Boot application uses its default logging starter, SLF4J events are handled by Logback. Common settings such as `logging.level.*`, `logging.file.name`, and groups belong in application properties or YAML. For Logback-specific appenders, rolling policy, encoders, or profiles, use `logback-spring.xml`; this applies only while Logback is the selected provider.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Boot starters normally select Logback through `spring-boot-starter-logging`
- Use `logging.level.*` and `logging.file.name` for common settings
- Use `logback-spring.xml` for Logback-specific appenders, encoders, and rolling policies
- The `-spring` name enables Boot's Logback extensions
- Choose retention and output rules for the deployment; there is no universal file policy

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In Spring Boot, logging is configured on two levels, and which one you use depends on how much control you need. By default Spring Boot ships with SLF4J as the API and Logback as the implementation, so you usually don't add any logging dependency at all. For the common cases, you configure everything in application.properties or application.yml. You set log levels with the logging.level prefix — logging.level.root equals INFO as a baseline, then raise your own packages to DEBUG. You can send logs to a file with logging.file.name, and you can customize the output pattern with logging.pattern.console. That handles the majority of what most apps need. When you need full control — things like rolling log files that archive daily and keep thirty days of history, multiple appenders, or JSON output for log aggregation — you add a logback configuration file. The important detail is to name it logback-spring.xml, with the dash spring suffix, rather than plain logback.xml. The spring-aware version lets Logback use Spring features like profiles, so you can say use a JSON file appender only in the prod profile, and console only in dev. Inside that XML you define appenders, where each appender is a destination — console, a rolling file, or a remote sink — and you attach them to loggers with specific levels. A common mistake is using a plain file appender with no rolling policy, because then the log file just grows until it fills the disk. So the short version is: properties for the simple, common settings, and logback-spring.xml when you need rolling files, multiple destinations, or profile-specific behavior.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Spring Boot starters normally bring `spring-boot-starter-logging`, which routes SLF4J to Logback. That default can be excluded and replaced, so configuration should match the provider actually on the classpath.

Provider-independent Boot settings handle common needs: `logging.level.com.example.orders=DEBUG`, `logging.level.root=INFO`, and `logging.file.name=logs/app.log`. Environment-specific values can come from normal Spring profiles and configuration sources.

Use `logback-spring.xml` when Logback features are needed, such as several appenders, a rolling policy, a structured encoder, or `<springProfile>` blocks. Prefer the `-spring` file name when using Boot's extensions because a plain `logback.xml` is loaded too early for some Spring features.

sections.title: Two Configuration Layers
sections.content:
blue|application.properties|~Quick + common|logging.level.*|logging.file.name|pattern tweaks
emerald|logback-spring.xml|~Full control|appenders|rolling policy|JSON encoder
amber|Profiles|~Per environment|<springProfile>|dev vs prod|different appenders
rose|Defaults|~Out of the box|console appender|INFO root|sensible pattern

sections.title: Common Config in application.properties
sections.content:
```properties
# Levels
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.bookstore=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=WARN

# Write to a file (rolls daily/size by default)
logging.file.name=logs/app.log

# Custom console + file patterns
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss} %-5level [%X{requestId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n
```

sections.title: Full Control with logback-spring.xml
sections.content:
```xml
<configuration>
  <appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
    <file>logs/app.log</file>
    <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">
      <fileNamePattern>logs/app.%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.log</fileNamePattern>
      <maxHistory>30</maxHistory>   <!-- keep 30 days -->
    </rollingPolicy>
    <encoder><pattern>%d %-5level %logger - %msg%n</pattern></encoder>
  </appender>

  <springProfile name="prod">       <!-- JSON only in prod -->
    <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="FILE"/></root>
  </springProfile>
</configuration>
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Naming it logback.xml when using Spring features**: use **logback-spring.xml** so `<springProfile>` and property substitution work.
- **No rolling policy**: a plain file appender grows unbounded until the disk fills.
- **Setting root to DEBUG**: floods logs with framework internals; raise only your own packages.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Application properties are easy to override per environment and cover common settings. `logback-spring.xml` offers deeper provider control but is more complex and specific to Logback. Container deployments often prefer structured stdout collected by the platform, while other systems may require managed files or archives.

questions.question: How do you add SLF4J logging to a Java class and write your first log statement?
questions.title: Adding SLF4J Logging to a Class
questions.direct_answer: Add `org.slf4j.Logger` and `LoggerFactory`, create a class-named logger, and write a parameterized event such as `log.info("User {} created", userId)`. Spring Boot applications commonly already have SLF4J and a provider through a starter; a plain Java project must declare the SLF4J API and exactly one compatible runtime provider.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Depend on the SLF4J API and use one compatible runtime provider
- Create a stable class-named logger with `LoggerFactory`
- Write parameterized events with `{}` placeholders
- Boot starters commonly supply SLF4J plus Logback; verify the actual dependency graph
- Lombok `@Slf4j` can generate the field but does not change logging behavior

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I import `Logger` and `LoggerFactory`, then declare `private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(UserService.class)`. The class argument creates a stable package-based logger name. A first event can be `log.info("User {} created", userId)`, using a placeholder instead of concatenation. In a typical Spring Boot application, an existing starter already brings SLF4J and the default Logback provider, but I verify the dependencies rather than assuming it. A plain Java application needs the SLF4J API and one compatible runtime provider. Lombok's `@Slf4j` is only a convenience that generates the same field.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Application code should depend on the SLF4J API. A typical class declares `private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(UserService.class)` and emits a parameterized event.

In a Spring Boot application, an ordinary starter usually supplies the SLF4J API and the default Logback provider. A minimal or deliberately reconfigured project may not, so check the dependency graph rather than assuming it.

A plain Java project needs `slf4j-api` plus one compatible provider at runtime. More than one provider can produce warnings and an unexpected selection; no provider means events are not handled as intended.

sections.title: Three Steps
sections.content:
blue|1. Import|~org.slf4j|Logger|LoggerFactory|API only
emerald|2. Declare|~static final|getLogger(X.class)|named by package|one per class
amber|3. Log|~with {}|log.info/debug/warn/error|placeholders|exception last
violet|Shortcut|~Lombok|@Slf4j on class|generates 'log'|less boilerplate

sections.title: From Imports to First Log Statement
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrong imports**: importing a logging implementation instead of `org.slf4j.*`.
- **Per-instance logger**: dropping `static`, creating a logger object per instance.
- **Concatenation**: `log.info("email=" + email)` instead of `log.info("email={}", email)`.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Writing the logger field explicitly has no Lombok requirement and makes the generated name visible. `@Slf4j` removes boilerplate but adds annotation processing. Either form produces normal SLF4J calls; the provider and runtime configuration still control output.

questions.question: How do you configure log levels in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Configuring Log Levels in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Set levels with `logging.level.<logger-name>=LEVEL` in Spring Boot configuration, for example `logging.level.com.example.orders=DEBUG`. Child loggers inherit an effective level unless overridden. The Actuator `loggers` endpoint can inspect or change levels at runtime when the actuator is present and the endpoint is deliberately exposed and secured; runtime changes may not survive restart.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Configure `logging.level.<logger-name>=LEVEL` in properties or YAML
- Package and class loggers inherit an effective level unless overridden
- Pick root and package levels for the environment; INFO is common, not mandatory
- Actuator can change levels only when present, exposed, and authorized
- Runtime changes need persistent configuration to survive restart

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring Boot accepts levels through `logging.level.<logger-name>`. For example, `logging.level.com.example.orders=DEBUG` enables more detail for one package while other loggers keep their inherited levels. The root level is an environment decision, not a fixed rule; I keep broad third-party logging conservative and temporarily raise only the logger being investigated. If Actuator is installed, its `loggers` endpoint can inspect and change levels at runtime, but the endpoint must be deliberately exposed and secured. An in-memory change normally disappears after restart unless the durable configuration is also updated.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Spring Boot maps `logging.level.<name>` to the selected logging system. The name can be the root logger, a package, or a class. For example, `logging.level.com.example.orders=DEBUG` affects that package hierarchy unless a child has its own setting.

Choose the root and package levels for each environment instead of treating INFO as a universal rule. Production may keep noisy framework packages at WARN while leaving application business events at INFO; a temporary diagnosis may enable DEBUG for one narrow logger.

With Actuator installed, the `loggers` endpoint can show effective levels and accept runtime changes. It is not exposed automatically in every deployment, should be protected as an operational control, and an in-memory change generally disappears when the application restarts.

sections.title: Level Configuration Strategy
sections.content:
blue|root=INFO|~Safe default|covers all libraries|keep conservative|baseline
emerald|your package=DEBUG|~Investigate|com.app|children inherit|raise on demand
amber|single class=TRACE|~Targeted|fully-qualified name|finest control|deep dive
violet|Actuator|~Runtime change|POST /actuator/loggers|no restart|incident-friendly

sections.title: Levels in Properties and YAML
sections.content:
```properties
# application.properties
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.bookstore=DEBUG
logging.level.com.bookstore.order.OrderService=TRACE
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=WARN
```

```yaml
# application-prod.yml — quieter in production
logging:
  level:
    root: WARN
    com.bookstore: INFO
```

sections.title: Change a Level at Runtime via Actuator
sections.content:
```bash
# Inspect current level
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.bookstore.order

# Raise to DEBUG live during an incident
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.bookstore.order \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'
# ...reproduce the bug, then POST {"configuredLevel":"INFO"} to revert.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`root=DEBUG`**: enables DEBUG for every dependency; logs become unreadable.
- **Leaving DEBUG in prod**: hurts performance and storage; revert after troubleshooting.
- **No profiles**: one file for all environments forces manual edits per deploy.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Broad DEBUG or TRACE can expose data, create volume, and slow a busy service. A narrow class/package override reduces that risk. Dynamic changes help incidents but are privileged operations and should be audited and returned to normal after diagnosis.

questions.question: Why does SLF4J use placeholder syntax ({}) instead of string concatenation for log messages?
questions.title: Why SLF4J Uses {} Placeholders
questions.direct_answer: SLF4J's `{}` placeholders let the provider format arguments only when the event is enabled, avoiding unconditional string concatenation and most unnecessary `toString()` calls. Java still evaluates arguments before calling the logger, so wrap genuinely expensive calculations with a level check or SLF4J 2's supplier-based fluent API. Placeholders also keep the message template separate from its values.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `{}` keeps the message template separate from argument values
- Disabled events normally skip formatting and argument `toString()` calls
- Java still evaluates method arguments before calling the logger
- Guard expensive calculations or use SLF4J 2 supplier arguments where supported
- A trailing `Throwable` is treated as an exception when not consumed by a placeholder

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: SLF4J uses curly-brace placeholders instead of string concatenation mainly for performance, and it comes down to when the string actually gets built. If you write log.debug of the literal cart equals plus cart, Java has to build that entire string — including calling cart.toString — before it even calls the log.debug method, because the argument is evaluated first. So if DEBUG is turned off in production, you've just done all that string-building work for a message that gets thrown away. On a hot code path that runs thousands of times, that's real wasted CPU. With the placeholder style — log.debug of cart equals curly-brace, passing cart as a separate argument — SLF4J first checks whether DEBUG is actually enabled, and only if it is does it substitute the argument and call toString. So the cost is deferred and, when the level is off, basically nothing happens. On top of the performance benefit, placeholders make the message more readable and they're null-safe — a null argument just prints as null rather than throwing. There's one extra refinement worth mentioning: the placeholder optimization defers stringifying the argument, but it doesn't defer evaluating an expensive method you pass in. If the argument itself is something costly to compute, like building a big snapshot object, you wrap the call in an if log.isDebugEnabled guard so that expensive method doesn't run when DEBUG is off. And for exceptions, you don't use a placeholder — you pass the exception as the last argument, and SLF4J prints the full stack trace.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
In `log.debug("Loaded order {}", order)`, SLF4J receives a message template and argument separately. If DEBUG is disabled, the provider can skip formatting the message and normally avoids calling `order.toString()`. Concatenation builds the string before the logging call and pays that cost whether the event is enabled or not.

Placeholders do not delay Java argument evaluation. `log.debug("Report {}", buildReport())` calls `buildReport()` first. Use `if (log.isDebugEnabled())` around expensive work, or the SLF4J 2 fluent API with a supplier when supported.

Parameterized logging also handles null arguments and recognizes a trailing `Throwable` for exception output when it is not consumed by a placeholder. Keep placeholder count and argument order clear so fields are not silently misplaced.

sections.title: Concatenation vs Placeholder
sections.content:
rose|Concatenation|~Cost paid always|toString() runs|even when level off|wasted CPU
emerald|{} placeholder|~Cost deferred|level checked first|stringify only if logged|fast when off
blue|Extra guard|~Very costly args|if(log.isDebugEnabled())|skip arg building|for heavy work

sections.title: Concatenation — Always Pays the Cost
Placeholders — Deferred and Clean
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Concatenating anyway**: `log.debug("x=" + obj)` defeats the optimization entirely.
- **Mixing both**: `log.info("id=" + id + " name={}", name)` — keep all values as placeholders.
- **Calling expensive methods as args** without an `isDebugEnabled()` guard — the method still runs.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Parameterized logging avoids unconditional formatting, but it does not make an expensive argument expression lazy. Supplier-based fluent calls can defer that work, while a simple level check is compatible with older APIs. Keep templates stable for search and structured processing.

questions.question: What is the difference between Logback and Log4j2 in Java?
questions.title: Logback vs Log4j2 in Java
questions.direct_answer: Logback and Log4j 2 are logging providers that can sit behind SLF4J. Spring Boot's default logging starter selects Logback; Boot can use Log4j 2 after replacing that starter. Both support filters, rolling files, structured layouts, and asynchronous options, with different configuration and performance characteristics. Choose for required features, ecosystem fit, and measurements from the application's workload—not a universal speed claim.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Both can serve as an SLF4J logging provider
- Spring Boot's default logging starter selects Logback
- Boot can select Log4j 2 by replacing the default starter
- Both offer rolling, filtering, structured output, and asynchronous options
- Compare required features and benchmark the real workload instead of assuming one is always faster

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Logback and Log4j 2 are runtime logging providers that can handle events sent through SLF4J. Spring Boot's default logging starter selects Logback. If a project chooses Log4j 2, it should exclude the default logging starter and add Boot's Log4j 2 starter so two providers do not compete. Both support levels, appenders, rolling files, structured output, filtering, and asynchronous designs, but their configuration models and details differ. Log4j 2 has its asynchronous logger architecture and plugin ecosystem; Logback has straightforward Boot integration and asynchronous appender support. I choose based on required features, operational familiarity, and measurements of the application's actual event volume and durability needs—not a universal speed claim.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
Both Logback and Log4j 2 can handle SLF4J events, format them, filter by level, and send them to appenders. A project should bind SLF4J to one intended provider and use the corresponding configuration files and extensions.

Spring Boot's normal logging starter uses Logback. To use Log4j 2, exclude the default logging starter and add `spring-boot-starter-log4j2`; simply adding another provider can create competing bindings.

Log4j 2 offers its own asynchronous logger architecture and plugin ecosystem. Logback also supports asynchronous appenders and has strong Boot integration. Throughput, latency, allocation, loss behavior, and shutdown guarantees depend on the exact configuration, so benchmark the application's real logging pattern before switching for performance.

sections.title: Logback vs Log4j2
sections.content:
emerald|Logback|~Spring Boot default|native to SLF4J|simple config|great for most apps
blue|Log4j2|~High throughput|async via Disruptor|lambda lazy logging|when logging is the bottleneck
amber|Same for you|~Both behind SLF4J|code unchanged|swap = dependency|one config style

sections.title: Key Differences
sections.content:
| Aspect | Logback | Log4j2 |
|---|---|---|
| Spring Boot default | Yes | No (opt-in) |
| Relationship to SLF4J | Native implementation | SLF4J-compatible |
| Async logging | AsyncAppender (good) | LMAX Disruptor (excellent) |
| Lazy messages | Via guards/placeholders | Lambda suppliers (`() -> ...`) |
| Config | logback-spring.xml | log4j2.xml / .yml |
| Best for | Most applications | Very high log throughput |

sections.title: Default — Logback (Spring Boot)
Switching to Log4j2 — Dependency Swap
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- Exclude the default Logback starter, add the Log4j2 starter -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-log4j2</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

The Java code above does not change — that's the SLF4J facade paying off.

sections.title: When to Choose Which
sections.content:
Keep Logback when it meets the application's formatting, routing, performance, and operational needs, especially in a standard Spring Boot setup. Choose Log4j 2 for a required feature or after a representative benchmark shows a useful improvement.

When switching in Spring Boot, replace the default starter rather than leaving two providers. Validate startup diagnostics, async queue behavior, shutdown flushing, rolling and retention, structured output, and failure behavior of the destination.

questions.question: What is MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) in Java logging and how is it used?
questions.title: MDC — Mapped Diagnostic Context in Java Logging
questions.direct_answer: SLF4J MDC exposes key-value diagnostic context normally associated with the current thread. Put a request or trace ID into the context and configure the provider's pattern or encoder to include it. MDC does not automatically follow work into thread pools, `CompletableFuture`, `@Async`, or reactive execution, so propagate context deliberately and restore or clear it on reusable threads.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- MDC holds diagnostic fields associated with the current execution thread
- A pattern such as `%X{requestId}` or structured encoder must render the field
- Executor and reactive boundaries need deliberate propagation support
- Restore or clear context on pooled threads to prevent cross-request leakage
- Keep identifiers safe; do not put secrets or large objects in MDC

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: MDC is a diagnostic key-value context exposed by SLF4J and supported by logging providers. A servlet filter can put a request ID into MDC before the chain, and a configured pattern such as `%X{requestId}` or a structured encoder can add it to later events. Setting a value alone does not force every output to print it. Traditional MDC is associated with the current thread, so an executor task, `CompletableFuture`, or reactive pipeline does not automatically inherit it. I use the framework's propagation mechanism for those boundaries. On a pooled thread I restore the previous context or clear my value in `finally`, otherwise the next request can receive the wrong ID.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
MDC lets code attach context such as `requestId` to logging events without repeating that value in every call. The active provider holds the context and an output pattern such as `%X{requestId}` or a structured encoder decides whether it appears.

Traditional MDC is thread-associated. A servlet filter can set the request ID before the chain and restore or clear it in `finally`. A pooled thread is reused, so a leaked value can label the next request incorrectly.

Async work needs explicit support. Copying the context map in a task decorator can work for an executor; reactive frameworks have their own context and bridging mechanisms. Preserve any previous MDC map as well as clearing newly added keys so nested scopes remain correct.

sections.title: MDC at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Thread-local map|~Per request|key-value pairs|set once|auto-attached
emerald|Use case|~Correlation|requestId / userId|trace one request|across classes
amber|Print it|~%X{key}|in the log pattern|or JSON field|every line
rose|Gotcha|~Must clear|MDC.clear() in finally|pooled threads reuse|stale values leak

sections.title: MDC in a Servlet Filter
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not clearing MDC**: leftover values leak into the next pooled request's logs — always `MDC.clear()` in `finally`.
- **Assuming it crosses threads**: MDC is thread-local; async tasks/new threads lose it unless you copy it over.
- **Storing large objects**: keep MDC to small identifiers, not whole payloads.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: MDC keeps call sites small, but implicit thread context is easy to lose across async boundaries and leak on pools. Explicit structured arguments are clearer for a one-off field. Use MDC for cross-cutting correlation data and propagate it with the execution model in use.
